# Efficient Fable

Use Claude Fable as the orchestrator, architect, synthesizer, and final judge.
Use cheaper subagents for token-heavy research, coding, testing, and
summarization that do not require Fable's full judgment.

## Where Fable Shines

Reserve Fable for:

- Decomposing ambiguous work into clean parallel slices.
- Architecture, product, and safety tradeoffs.
- Reading conflicting subagent reports and deciding what matters.
- Integrating partial implementations into one coherent plan.
- Final review, risk assessment, and user-facing synthesis.

## Delegation Pattern

1. Name the expensive-token risk: large repo search, long logs, broad docs, or
   repetitive edits.
2. Split independent work into subagents before reading everything yourself.
3. Use cheaper models for research scans, inventory, search summaries, narrow
   bug hunts, browser/testing passes, test output reduction, and bounded code
   edits.
4. Ask subagents for concise evidence: files, line references, commands run,
   diffs, uncertainties, and stop conditions they hit.
5. Spend Fable tokens on the decision layer: compare results, resolve conflicts,
   choose the implementation path, and review the final patch.

Prefer parallel subagents when the slices do not depend on each other. Keep
blocking or highly coupled work local.

## Handoff Packets

Write delegated prompts as if the subagent has no useful chat context. Include
only the context it needs:

- The repo path and exact objective.
- The files, packages, or surfaces in scope and anything explicitly out of
  scope.
- The evidence format to return: files, line refs, commands, diffs, failures,
  screenshots, and uncertainty.
- The verification commands or browser flows to run, plus what success should
  look like when that is knowable.
- Stop conditions: if the code does not match the prompt, a command fails after
  a reasonable retry, or the task needs out-of-scope files, stop and report
  instead of improvising.

## Vetting Delegated Work

Treat subagent reports as leads, not facts. Before using a high-impact finding,
opening a PR, or telling the user the work is done, Fable should reopen the
important cited files, confirm the relevant line refs or failures, and review
the final diff against the task. Let lighter agents gather signal; keep
truth-judgment with Fable.

## Common Scenarios

Treat these as soft defaults, not rigid rules:

- Research: ask lighter agents to scan docs, prior art, APIs, and repo surfaces;
  Fable decides what evidence changes the plan.
- Coding: give cheaper agents bounded edits or candidate patches; Fable owns
  shared-file coordination, integration, and final review.
- Testing: have Fable suggest the validation direction and the scripts or
  browser checks that matter. Let lighter agents run targeted tests, browser
  flows, screenshots, and log reduction, then report exact commands, failures,
  likely causes, and whether failures look flaky, environmental, or real.
- Debugging: use cheaper agents to cluster logs, reproduce issues, and try
  small fixes; Fable decides which diagnosis is most trustworthy.

If a task is tiny or the validation itself needs delicate judgment, keep it
with Fable.

## Diagram

Use `assets/fable-orchestrator.excalidraw` when a visual explanation helps.

## Claims

For codebase-heavy work, it is reasonable to describe this as up to 3-5x more
cost-efficient and 2-4x faster when independent research, coding, or testing
slices can run in parallel. Treat those as workload-dependent estimates, not
guarantees.

Good launch copy:

> Make Claude Fable more efficient by using cheaper subagents for token-heavy
> research, coding, and testing, saving Fable for judgment, architecture,
> synthesis, and final review.

- codex: Delegate a scoped, self-contained coding task to OpenAI's Codex CLI (`codex exec`) as a one-shot: hand it a tight spec, let it edit files in the repo, then review and integrate the result. Use when the user explicitly asks to "use codex", wants an OpenAI/GPT model to do a coding task, wants a second implementation to compare against, or when a task is well-specified enough to farm out non-interactively. Not for open-ended exploration.
- cross-review: Review code with the model that did NOT write it. Attributes each changed file to Claude, Codex, or a human (via git trailers + Claude/Codex transcripts on disk), then routes Claude-written code to `codex exec` and Codex-written code to a fresh `claude -p`, runs both in parallel, and merges the findings. Use when the user asks for a cross-model / second-model review, wants "codex to review this", wants an independent reviewer that didn't author the code, or asks who wrote a diff. For a normal same-model review use /code-review.
- dev-server-check: Check whether a dev server is already running for this project before starting one, and reuse it instead of spawning a duplicate. Use BEFORE any command that starts a long-running local server — npm/pnpm/yarn/bun run dev|start|serve, vite, next dev, wrangler dev, nodemon, tsx watch, uvicorn, rails s, expo, python -m http.server — and whenever you need the URL/port of "the app" to open, curl, or screenshot it. Also use when a port is unexpectedly taken, when a change is not showing up in the browser, or when the user asks what is running locally.
- dev-server-cleanup: Find and kill duplicate, stale, or orphaned local dev servers and free ports that are stuck in use. Use when the user says a port is already in use, asks to clean up / kill dev servers, notices many node or vite processes running, wants to know what is listening on a port, or after a session leaves stray background servers behind. Worktree-aware: it never treats servers from different git worktrees of the same repo as duplicates.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- durable-objects: Create and review Cloudflare Durable Objects. Use when building stateful coordination (chat rooms, multiplayer games, booking systems), implementing RPC methods, SQLite storage, alarms, WebSockets, or reviewing DO code for best practices. Covers Workers integration, wrangler config, and testing with Vitest. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- efficient-fable: Use when running Claude Fable on codebase-heavy or token-heavy work and the user wants Fable to orchestrate research, coding, and testing while cheaper subagents do bounded heavy lifting.
- efficient-fable-measured: Fable delegation with measured per-model routing, an OpenAI Codex executor lane, and a way to check the routing against real cost. Use when the user names it explicitly, or asks to route delegated work by model/cost, to use gpt-5.6-sol as an executor, or to see what subagents actually cost. For generic Fable delegation guidance the default skill is `efficient-fable`.

Use when building outreach lists and a contact's email is unknown. Sibling to github-email; reach for it when the target is a researcher (papers), an OSS/package author (npm/PyPI/lore), or when you only have a name + company domain. Input is a name, arxiv id, package, url, or handle; output is candidate emails.

- lead-qualification: Find, qualify, score, and rank B2B leads (design partners, buyers, hires, advisors) using the local lead-engine (Fit x Intent model). - sandbox-sdk: Build sandboxed applications for secure code execution. # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. ## Summary of findings

### 1. Where terminal text arrives — shape

- **`ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:412-432`** — `readSurfaceText(_:lines:)` sends WS command `surface.read_text` (comment at 404-411 explains it returns "the last `lines` rows *including terminal scrollback*"). The completion handler reads `result["text"] as? String` (line 418) — a **single `String`**, not an array of lines or attributed runs.
- **`ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:489-500`** (`trimTerminalText`) — splits that string on `"\n"` (`omittingEmptySubsequences: false`), trims trailing whitespace per line, drops trailing blank lines, and rejoins with `"\n"`. Purely line-oriented; **no distinction between a hard newline and a terminal soft-wrap** — it only ever sees `\n` characters, one flavor.
- **`ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:506-510`** (`capHistoryLines`) — bounds total line count, same `\n`-split model.
- Result is stored in `@Published var surfaceContent: [String: String]`, then flows to the view via **`ios/cmux/Layout/WorkspaceLayoutView.swift:517` and `:585`**: `terminalText: ... (appState.surfaceContent[surface.id] ?? "")`.
- Confirmed wire shape independently: **`bridge/internal/socket/client_test.go:79-101`** — the bridge's fake-cmux test responds with `{"id":...,"ok":true,"result":{"text":"hello"}}`. No wrap flags, no per-row metadata in the payload shape this repo knows about.

### 2. Where links are detected/made tappable

All in **`ios/cmux/Layout/TerminalTextView.swift`**:
- Line 37-39 comment: explicitly **not** using `UITextView.dataDetectorTypes` ("Links come from our own detector pass in `TerminalTextRenderer`, not `dataDetectorTypes`") — done off-main to avoid UIKit's synchronous whole-document rescan.
- **Line 215-216**: `private static let linkDetector: NSDataDetector? = try? NSDataDetector(types: NSTextCheckingResult.CheckingType.link.rawValue)`.
- **Line 229-259**: `addLinks(to:trimTrailingJunk:)` runs the detector **once over the entire `attr.string`** (`detector.matches(in: attr.string, range: NSRange(location: 0, length: ns.length))`, line 232) — this string still contains the real `\n` characters from the terminal's hard-wrapped rows. `NSDataDetector`'s `.link` matcher does not span a newline, so a URL broken across two terminal rows (e.g. `...business_os_landscap\ne.html`) produces at most a match ending at `landscap` (truncated) and a separate/no match for `e.html`.
- **Line 200-213** (`TerminalTextRenderer.build`): builds the `NSAttributedString` from `snapshot.text` (the same possibly-wrapped string) and calls `addLinks` — the two call sites are `PaneCardView.swift:123` (live terminal pane, `trimMarkdownLinks: false`) and `PaneCardView.swift:302` (Claude transcript viewer, `trimMarkdownLinks: true`).
- Tap handling: `Coordinator` (line 64) conforms to `UITextViewDelegate` but implements no `shouldInteractWith`/`primaryActionFor` override (verified via repo-wide grep — no match), so tapping a `.link`-attributed range uses UIKit's default open-URL behavior; there is no `.environment(\.openURL)`/SwiftUI `Link` involved anywhere in this flow.

### 3. Bridge's knowledge of wrap vs. hard newline

- **`bridge/internal/ws/handler.go:207-231`** (`proxyCommand`) — for every method except `claude.transcript`, including `surface.read_text`, the bridge is a **transparent pass-through**: `client.Send(cmd.Method, cmd.Params)` forwards params to cmux's own Unix-socket RPC and relays the raw `result` bytes back unmodified. There is no bridge-side transformation, joining, or wrap-flag extraction for `surface.read_text` anywhere in `bridge/internal/{ws,socket,poller}`.
- Confirmed no other file touches this text: `grep -rn "read_text|surface_content"` across `bridge/internal` only turns up the pass-through test (`socket/client_test.go`); `bridge/internal/poller/poller.go:19` only has a `SurfaceID` field for *notifications*, unrelated to terminal text content.
- **`bridge/internal/claude/transcript.go:264`** (`renderJSONL`) is a different code path entirely — it renders Claude session `.jsonl` message content to markdown text for `claude.transcript`, not a PTY screen capture, so it isn't subject to column-width hard-wrapping the same way (its long lines, if any, come from the source content, not terminal wrapping).
- No trace of terminal column width/`cols` anywhere in this repo (`grep -rn "cols|width" bridge/internal ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift` turns up unrelated SwiftUI/CGRect frame code only) — **neither the bridge nor the iOS app has access to the PTY's column count**, so nothing here could reliably tell "line N was cut because it hit column 80" from "line N is just a short line." That knowledge lives inside cmux's terminal emulator itself, which is external to this repo. Trailing padding on wrapped rows, if cmux emits any, is stripped anyway by `trimTerminalText` (AppState.swift:492-494) before the text ever reaches the renderer/detector.

### 4. Uncommitted diffs — not link-related

`git diff` on the four modified files shows a self-contained, unrelated in-flight feature: **distinguishing "this surface's bound Claude session `.jsonl` file is missing from disk" from "no conversation yet"** in the Claude transcript/history viewer.

- `bridge/internal/claude/transcript.go`: `Resolver.Render` refactored to return a `Result` struct with a new `SessionMissing bool` field; `resolveTranscriptPath` now returns `boundSession` and, when `checkpoint_id` is well-formed but its `.jsonl` file isn't found, deliberately returns early instead of falling back to the cwd heuristic (to avoid showing a *different* surface's conversation).
- `bridge/internal/ws/handler.go:194-199`: adds `"session_missing": res.SessionMissing` to the `claude.transcript` JSON result.
- `ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:46-49, 288, 462-473`: adds `@Published var claudeTranscriptMissing: Set<String>`, populates it from the new `session_missing` field.
- `ios/cmux/Layout/PaneCardView.swift:283-293`: adds a "This surface's session file is missing" message in the transcript sheet's empty state.

None of this touches `TerminalTextView.swift`, `NSDataDetector`, `surface.read_text`, or `surfaceContent`/`terminalText`. **This WIP work is orthogonal to the URL-wrap bug** — confirming the task's implicit assumption does not hold (these diffs are not the link-detection code path).

## Data flow (bug path)

cmux (external, wraps PTY output at terminal column width, opaque to this repo) → `surface.read_text` RPC → `bridge/internal/ws/handler.go:207` `proxyCommand` (pure pass-through, no wrap awareness) → WS event → `AppState.swift:417-431` `readSurfaceText` → `trimTerminalText`/`capHistoryLines` (line-split on `\n`, no join) → `surfaceContent[surfaceID]` → `WorkspaceLayoutView.swift:517/585` → `PaneCardView.swift:123` `terminalText:` → `TerminalTextView.swift:200` `TerminalTextRenderer.build` → `addLinks` (line 229-259) running `NSDataDetector` over the whole (still-wrapped) string → truncated/broken link at the wrap point.

## Candidate fix locations

- **iOS-side, in `TerminalTextRenderer` (`ios/cmux/Layout/TerminalTextView.swift:200-259`)** — most tractable given available data: before/instead of running `NSDataDetector` on `snapshot.text` verbatim, build a link-detection pass that treats certain `\n` boundaries as joinable (e.g., a heuristic: line ends with URL-safe characters and no trailing whitespace/punctuation, next line starts immediately with more URL-safe characters), detect on the joined text, then map matched ranges back to offsets in the *original* string before calling `attr.addAttribute(.link, range:)` at line 257 — so the visible line breaks (matching the actual terminal layout) are preserved but the tappable link spans the full URL. This is necessarily a **content heuristic**, not a precise wrap/hard-newline distinction, because column-width info isn't available here.
- **Not `AppState.trimTerminalText`/`surfaceContent`** — joining lines at that layer would corrupt the displayed terminal output (which must visually match the real terminal at its actual column width), so any fix must be confined to the link-detection pass, not the stored/displayed text.
- **Bridge-side unwrap (`bridge/internal/ws/handler.go` `proxyCommand`, or a dedicated `surface.read_text` handler)** — would be the more "correct" place if cmux's own RPC exposed wrap metadata (e.g., a per-row wrap flag or an "unwrapped" text variant), but nothing in this repo's bridge currently receives or requests such metadata; `surface.read_text` is a dumb proxy today (handler.go:207-231), and cmux itself is out of this repo's tree. A bridge fix is blocked on either cmux's protocol exposing wrap info or the bridge adopting the same content-heuristic approach — it has no more information than the iOS client does.

## Uncertainties

- Whether cmux's `surface.read_text` RPC has any additional/optional params (e.g., requesting unwrapped text, or a `cols` field) is unknown — this repo only shows the bridge calling `client.Send(cmd.Method, cmd.Params)` generically; cmux's actual RPC surface lives outside this repo and wasn't available to inspect.
- Whether cmux pads wrapped rows with trailing spaces couldn't be directly confirmed (opaque upstream), but it's moot for a fix since `trimTerminalText` (AppState.swift:489-500) already strips trailing whitespace per line before the text is used anywhere.
- The Claude transcript viewer path (`PaneCardView.swift:302`, `trimMarkdownLinks: true`) uses the same `addLinks` function but its text comes from `renderJSONL` (message content, not PTY capture) — plausibly not exposed to this specific wrap bug, though not exhaustively verified since `renderJSONL`'s internals weren't fully read.

204	            string: snapshot.text,

219	    /// but that aren't part of it. Data detectors grab them greedily — e.g.
220	    /// `**https://example.com/x**` yields `https://example.com/x**`, so the tap
221	    /// opens a broken URL. `)` is handled separately to preserve balanced parens.
222	    private static let trailingJunk = CharacterSet(charactersIn: "*_~`.,;:!?\"']}>")

227	    /// detector's own match and URL are used verbatim (live terminal cards,
228	    /// matching what UITextView's built-in link detection produced).
229	    private static func addLinks(to attr: NSMutableAttributedString, trimTrailingJunk trim: Bool) {
230	        guard let detector = linkDetector else { return }
231	        let ns = attr.string as NSString
232	        let matches = detector.matches(in: attr.string, range: NSRange(location: 0, length: ns.length))

234	            var range = match.range
235	            var url = match.url
236	            if trim {
237	                while range.length > 0 {
238	                    let unit = ns.character(at: range.location + range.length - 1)
239	                    guard let scalar = Unicode.Scalar(unit) else { break }
240	                    if scalar == ")" {
241	                        // Keep a ) that closes a ( inside the URL (e.g.
242	                        // wiki/Foo_(bar)) — but trim unbalanced extras, as in
243	                        // "(see wiki/Foo_(bar))" where the last ) is prose.
244	                        let candidate = ns.substring(with: range)
245	                        let opens = candidate.lazy.filter { $0 == "(" }.count
246	                        let closes = candidate.lazy.filter { $0 == ")" }.count
247	                        if closes <= opens { break }
248	                    } else if !trailingJunk.contains(scalar) {
249	                        break
250	                    }
251	                    range.length -= 1
252	                }
253	                guard range.length > 0 else { continue }
254	                url = URL(string: ns.substring(with: range))
255	            }
256	            guard let url else { continue }
257	            attr.addAttribute(.link, value: url, range: range)
258	        }
259	    }

## What changed

**1. Tab key** — `TerminalInputBar.swift`: the bar already had a `⇥` chip, but only while the compose field was focused (keyboard up). There's now an always-visible `⇥` button on the collapsed input bar, so Tab is one tap away without raising the keyboard. It sends the same `surface.send_key "Tab"` the existing chip uses.

**2. "Working" indicator on surfaces** — no busy signal exists anywhere in the cmux protocol, so I derived one client-side: a surface is "working" when its most recent `surface.read_text` poll saw the screen change (TUIs like Claude Code repaint continuously while running and go static when idle). 
- `AppState.swift`: new `@Published workingSurfaces: Set<String>`, updated inside the existing poll diff-guard; polls at a different read depth (focus flips 50-line previews to deep reads) don't count as activity, so focus switches don't cause false blips. Sending text or a key also schedules a one-off probe read 1.5s later, so after you send a message the indicator reacts in ~1.5s instead of waiting for the next poll.
- `PaneCardView.swift`: three green pulsing dots in the card title bar (next to where the REC badge lives), on both the focused card and secondary tiles.
- Known limits: background tiles only poll every ~15s, so their indicator updates on that cadence between sends; and a silent long-running command (no output) reads as idle.

**3. Swipe vs. text selection** — `TerminalTextView` now implements `textViewDidChangeSelection` and reports select/deselect transitions up through `PaneCardView` to `WorkspaceLayoutView`, where the cycle-swipe `DragGesture` vetoes itself while a selection is active. One deliberate behavior: while text is selected, swipes won't switch surfaces at all — tap to deselect, then swipe. The flag resets on surface change so a stale selection can't wedge the gesture.

**4. Hard-wrapped links** — in `TerminalTextRenderer.addLinks`, a URL match that runs to the edge of a full-width row (the longest row in the snapshot, min 40 chars — the PTY width isn't in the protocol) and continues with URL characters on the next row is now joined into a single tappable link spanning the visual break, with the newline removed from the actual URL. The tail fragment can't double-linkify. Verified offline against your exact `business_os_landscap` / `e.html` example, a three-row wrap, and three no-false-positive cases — all pass. The transcript viewer path is untouched (its text is logical lines, never width-wrapped). Edge case that stays broken: a URL wrapped mid-hostname before the TLD (the detector can't match the first fragment at all).

# Cross-model code review

A model reviewing its own output is a weak check: it repeats the assumptions it
made while writing. This skill breaks that loop by routing every slice of a diff
to the model that **didn't** write it.

```
diff ──┬─ Claude-authored ──────────► codex exec      (OpenAI reviews Anthropic)
       ├─ Codex-authored ───────────► claude -p       (Anthropic reviews OpenAI)
       └─ human / unattributable ───► codex exec      (opposite of this session)
              each side × N lenses         │
                                           ▼
                                   merged + deduped findings
                                           │
                                           ▼
                          verify.py: one throwaway worktree per finding,
                          reproduce it by RUNNING code (not the raiser,
                          not the author) ──► reproduced / refuted / inconclusive
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                   you fix ──► record.py (next run learns)
```

Reviewers run **concurrently** and **read-only**; verification runs in
disposable git worktrees that never touch the real repo. You (the session agent)
own the fixes and the report.

## Preflight

1. **Both CLIs must be present.** `codex --version` and `claude --version`. If
   `codex` is missing, tell the user to install and sign in — don't do it
   yourself:
   > Codex CLI isn't installed. Install with `npm i -g @openai/codex`, then sign
   > in with `codex login`. Ping me when done.
   Stop and wait.
2. **Must be a git repo.** Attribution is diff-based; there is no scope without
   one.
3. **Note a dirty tree** if reviewing a committed scope, so the user knows the
   working-tree changes aren't included.

## Step 1 — attribute the diff

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/attribute.py --repo "$REPO"
```

Scope flags (default is `--uncommitted`):

| Flag | Scope |
|---|---|
| `--uncommitted` | staged + unstaged + untracked (default) |
| `--base main` | merge-base of `main`..HEAD — the branch's work |
| `--commit SHA` | one commit |
| `--range A..B` | an explicit revision range |

Other flags: `--days N` (transcript lookback, default 30), `--all-projects`
(force-scan every Claude project dir), `--mixed both` (files both agents touched
go to *both* reviewers instead of the opposite-of-dominant one),
`--session-agent codex` (set when Codex is driving, so human code routes to
Claude).

**How attribution works**, strongest signal first:

1. **Git trailers** (committed scopes) — Claude Code stamps
   `Co-Authored-By: Claude … <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Codex stamps nothing, so
   a Codex-written commit is identified via transcripts, not trailers.
2. **Transcripts on disk** — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/*.jsonl` (Edit/Write
   tool calls) and `~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl` (`patch_apply_end`
   change maps, `apply_patch` envelopes, and shell redirect writes). Paths
   resolve against each session's `cwd`. Codex's record format has changed
   across versions, so all three forms are parsed.
3. **Nothing found** → `unknown`, routed as human.

Each file comes back with `author`, `confidence`, `reviewer`, and `evidence`.
**Show the user the attribution table before reviewing** — it's often the most
interesting output, and a wrong call there sends the diff to the wrong model.

## Step 2 — dispatch both reviewers

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/attribute.py --repo "$REPO" --json \
  | python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/dispatch.py
```

This builds a per-slice diff, runs `codex exec --sandbox read-only` and
`claude -p --allowed-tools Read Grep Glob` in parallel — **each as a swarm of
lens-specific agents** — and merges their structured findings sorted by
severity. Add `--keep-raw` to retain raw reviewer output for debugging and
`--timeout N` (default 900s) for big diffs.

### The swarm — lenses, not one generalist

One generalist reviewer per side hits a breadth ceiling: it finds the loudest
defect in a file and moves on. So each side runs the **same diff** through
several agents that each carry a different question:

| Lens | Asks |
|---|---|
| `correctness` (default) | does this compute the wrong answer? boundaries, inverted conditions, state transitions, empty/null/negative inputs |
| `security` (default) | who can reach this with hostile input? authz, injection, timing-unsafe compares, secrets, traversal, missing limits |
| `concurrency-resources` (default) | unawaited promises, TOCTOU, mutation during iteration, leaked handles, missing cleanup on the error path, unbounded growth |
| `contracts` (opt-in) | do the two sides of each boundary agree on types, nullability, units, ordering? swallowed errors, half-written state, non-idempotent retries |

`--lenses a,b,c` picks the set; `--lenses none` runs the old single generalist
pass. Default is 3 lenses × 2 sides = **6 concurrent agents on one diff** —
that is the cost of the swarm, and `--lenses none` is the cheap mode for a small
or low-stakes diff. `agents_run` in the output says how many actually ran.

Findings are then **deduped across lenses**. Two findings merge when they are in
the same file within 3 lines, name ≥2 of the same code identifiers (backticked
spans, camelCase, snake_case — prose varies, symbol names don't), **and** their
defect kinds don't contradict. That last gate matters: every lens looking at one
broken function names the same symbols, so without it an unawaited promise, an
unhandled rejection, an unbounded fan-out and a missing authz check on the same
line collapse into one finding with four different fixes (observed, then fixed).
Merged findings carry `raised_by: N`, the lenses that saw it, and every other
description under `corroborating_summaries`. `raised` vs `after_dedupe` shows
how much overlap there was.

- **`raised_by > 1` is the swarm's strongest signal** — agents asking different
  questions converged on one defect. Lead with those and say so.
- **Always read `corroborating_summaries` on a merged finding.** Clustering is
  lexical and the defect-kind gate only recognises common kinds, so a *related
  but distinct* defect can still land in the same cluster. If a corroborating
  summary describes a different failure, split it back out and report it
  separately. Nothing is discarded — but nothing is verified either.

### Repo context — what the diff doesn't show

Reviewers also get a **usage pack** built alongside the diff: the symbols this
diff declares or changes, grepped for their call sites elsewhere in the repo
(`file:line`, capped at 12 symbols × 6 sites). This is the cheap local analogue
of Greptile's repo graph — a reviewer with the callers in hand checks whether
the change breaks them; a reviewer that has to go looking usually doesn't.
`--no-context` skips it.

Reviews take minutes on a real diff — **run this in the background and poll**
rather than blocking.

If a reviewer fails, its error lands in `errors` while the other's findings
still come through. Report partial results honestly; never present a one-sided
review as a full cross-review.

### Models — the thing that decides whether this is worth running

Two frontier reasoning models arguing about a diff is a real check. A mini-tier
model on either side still emits confident-sounding findings, so a downgrade is
invisible in the output — it just turns into noise you then have to verify. The
script therefore **pins models rather than inheriting CLI defaults**:

| Reviewer | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Claude | `--model opus --effort high` | the alias resolves to the latest Opus, so it never goes stale; `claude -p` would otherwise follow whatever the user last picked in `/model` |
| Codex | `gpt-5.6-sol` at `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | the flagship coding model. A configured model is respected only if it is the **same generation or newer** and not a cheap tier |

The Codex floor is **generation-aware**, not just a name blocklist — a whole
generation is a bigger quality gap than any prompt tuning:

- `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.5` → upgraded (older generation than `gpt-5.6`)
- `gpt-5.6-luna`, anything `mini/nano/lite/flash/…` → upgraded (cheap tier)
- `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-5.6-sol`, `gpt-5.7`, `gpt-6.x` → kept as configured

**Pinning the effort matters as much as pinning the model here: `gpt-5.6-sol`'s
own default reasoning level is `low`.** Asking the flagship for a review without
an explicit effort gets you its cheapest thinking. Sol and Terra also support
`xhigh`, `max`, and `ultra` above `high` — reach for `--codex-effort xhigh` on a
gnarly diff.

Overrides: `--codex-model` / `--claude-model`, `--codex-effort` /
`--claude-effort`. Use `--claude-model fable` for the hardest diffs. The resolved
model, effort, and where each came from are echoed to stderr at launch and
recorded in the output JSON under `reviewers` — **quote them in your report** so
a silent downgrade is visible.

When new models ship, update `CODEX_STRONG_DEFAULT` / `CODEX_MIN_GENERATION` at
the top of `dispatch.py`. To see what the installed CLI actually supports rather
than guessing: `strings -a /Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex |
rg -o 'gpt-5\.[0-9]+(-[a-z]+)?' | sort -u`, and the same dump carries each
model's `supported_reasoning_levels` and `context_window`.

## Step 3 — verify by execution

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/verify.py --repo "$REPO" --findings review.json
```

Each qualifying finding gets its **own disposable git worktree** (uncommitted
state applied, untracked files copied, `node_modules`/`.venv`/`vendor` symlinked
in) and its own agent, told to write a minimal reproduction, **run it**, and
return the command plus real output. Verdicts are `reproduced` / `refuted` /
`inconclusive`, written back onto each finding as a `verification` block with
`what_i_ran` and `observed`.

The verifier is the model that didn't write the code **and** isn't the one that
raised the finding, so a confabulated bug has to survive an independent attempt
to make it happen. Nothing touches the real repo — the worktrees are removed
afterwards.

Defaults: top 6 findings at medium+ severity and confidence (`--max`,
`--min-severity`, `--min-confidence`, `--all`). Anything skipped is announced on
stderr — **an unverified finding must never be reported as checked**.

Read the verdicts critically rather than trusting the label:

- `reproduced` with real output in `observed` — this is the strongest evidence
  the pipeline produces. Treat it as confirmed.
- `refuted` — believe it only if `what_i_ran` actually exercises the claimed
  path. A repro that stubbed away the interesting part refutes nothing. **Check
  the verdict against its own `observed` output**: a verifier that ran two
  variants and reports the passing one has refuted nothing. This is the observed
  failure mode — a real unawaited-promise bug came back `refuted` because a
  synchronously-resolving mock hid it, while the same run's timer-based variant
  printed the empty array that proves it. The prompt now forbids instant stubs
  for async claims, but read the evidence anyway.
- `inconclusive` — the claim is **unproven**, not "probably real". Say so.

`inconclusive` is the normal verdict for anything needing a live service, a
browser, or a full build, so expect it and fall back to Step 3b for those.

## Step 3b — verify by reading, when execution can't settle it

The findings are **claims from another model, not facts**. A reviewer that
didn't write the code also doesn't know the code's context, and cross-model
review produces confident-sounding false positives about intentional behavior.

For anything Step 3 left `inconclusive`, or skipped:

- Open the file and trace the actual code path; check the claimed failure
  scenario really occurs — inputs, state, ordering.
- Rule out the usual false positives: behavior guaranteed by a caller, an
  invariant enforced elsewhere, a deliberate choice the surrounding code makes,
  or an "unhandled" case that is genuinely unreachable.
- If you can settle it by running something yourself, do that instead — Step 3's
  cap and gates are budget decisions, not judgments about what's checkable.
- Drop anything you can't confirm. Say how many you dropped and why, and say
  which survivors were **reproduced by execution** versus confirmed by reading.
  Those are different strengths of evidence and the report must not blur them.

Note the asymmetry in what the reviewers themselves could do: `codex exec
--sandbox read-only` can run commands, while the Claude reviewer gets only
Read/Grep/Glob. Pass `--claude-bash` to give it command access too — useful on
a repo with a fast test suite, but it lets that subprocess run arbitrary
commands in the repo, so it is opt-in.

## Step 4 — fix and report

**Auto-fix** a finding only when **all** of these hold:

- the reviewer marked it `confidence: high`, **and**
- it was **`reproduced`** in Step 3, or you independently confirmed it yourself
  in Step 3b — an `inconclusive` verdict is not a confirmation, **and**
- the fix is local and unambiguous — a missing `await`, an off-by-one, a
  timing-unsafe comparison, an unchecked null. One obvious correct answer.

**Never auto-fix**: anything touching public API shape, schema/migrations, auth
or crypto policy, concurrency design, deletions of existing behavior, or
anything where two reasonable fixes exist. Those go to the user as open items
with a recommendation.

After applying fixes, **run the repo's tests/build/linter** if it has them, and
report the actual result. Show the user the diff of what you changed.

### Record the verdicts — this is what makes the next run better

Once you know what was real, write it back. Otherwise the same false positive
returns every run and you learn to skim the output:

```bash
echo '[{"file":"src/cache.py","line":9,"category":"correctness",
       "summary":"time.time() used for TTL","outcome":"dropped",
       "reason":"cache is advisory and process-local; monotonic not required"},
      {"file":"src/auth.ts","line":42,"category":"security",
       "summary":"token compared with ==","outcome":"fixed"}]' \
  | python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/record.py --repo "$REPO"
```

`outcome` is `dropped` (false positive), `confirmed`, or `fixed`. Record **every**
finding you adjudicated, dropped ones especially — a rejection without a `reason`

summary: Untrusted terminal output can make a displayed trusted URL navigate to a different host.
failure_scenario: A terminal prints a longest row of 40 characters consisting of 17 spaces followed by `https://trusted.example`, then a new row beginning `@evil.example`. The wrap heuristic removes the newline and constructs `https://trusted.example@evil.example`; UIKit interprets `trusted.example` as userinfo and navigates to `evil.example` when tapped, despite the prominent first row appearing to name the trusted host.
suggested_fix: Do not infer URL continuations across logical newlines without terminal soft-wrap metadata. At minimum, parse both URLs and reject a join unless the final scheme and host exactly match the original detected URL, preventing continuations from changing the authority.
category: URL injection / link spoofing

=== [1] ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:419 (medium/high, raised_by=1)
summary: Every input schedules an independent, non-cancellable activity probe.
failure_scenario: Rapidly tapping Tab, arrows, or another control key queues one delayed closure and one `surface.read_text` RPC per tap. When they fire together, the bridge's serial command handler and the client's pending-completion map accumulate a backlog, delaying subsequent input and consuming memory. The callbacks also survive bridge or workspace switches and can probe an obsolete surface through the new connection.
suggested_fix: Keep one cancellable/debounced probe per surface, replacing the previous pending probe on each input. Cancel all probes when resetting or changing the connection, and validate a connection/session generation before sending.
category: unbounded asynchronous work

=== [2] ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:456 (medium/high, raised_by=1)
summary: Detached poll processing can apply terminal snapshots out of order.
failure_scenario: Two same-depth polls return old content C1 and newer content C2. Because each response starts an independent detached task, C2 can finish first and set the content to C2, followed by C1 rolling it back. The next idle poll then compares C2 against the rolled-back C1 and reports the surface as working; for a background surface this can leave stale content and a false working indicator through another 15-second polling cycle.
suggested_fix: Assign a monotonically increasing request generation per surface before sending each read and discard processed results older than the latest accepted generation, or serialize processing per surface.
category: ordering race

suggested_fix: Capture the surface's current/last read depth when scheduling the probe, or explicitly compare the probe against a baseline read made at the same depth.
category: incorrect state transition
